key_facts: Searching algorithms are designed to check for or retrieve an element from a data structure, and are classified into two categories: Sequential Search and Interval Search.
Linear Search starts from the leftmost element of the list, compares the target x with each element one by one, returning the index if matched or -1 if no element matches.
Interval Search algorithms are specifically designed for searching in sorted data structures.
The hash table section covers basic concepts, direct-address tables, hash tables, hash functions, and open addressing as a collision-resolution technique.

The document is authored by Tran Ngoc Bao Duy from the Faculty of Computer Science and Engineering, Ho Chi Minh University of Technology, VNU-HCM, as Chapter 7 of a Data Structures and Algorithms course.
generated_text: Introduction to Searching and Hashing In data structures, finding or retrieving an element efficiently is a fundamental operation. This lesson introduces two important concepts for this purpose: Searching Algorithms and Hash Tables. Searching Algorithms are designed to check for an element or retrieve an element from any data structure where it is stored. We will explore two main categories of these algorithms. A Hash Table is a data structure that uses a special function, called a hash function, to map keys to values, allowing for very fast lookups. We will look at a common method for creating these functions. Searching Algorithms Based on the type of search operation, these algorithms are generally classified into two categories: Sequential Search: In this, the list or array is traversed sequentially and every element is checked. Interval Search: These algorithms are specifically designed for searching in sorted data-structures. Sequential Search: Linear Search The most straightforward sequential search is the Linear Search. Approach: Start from the leftmost element of the list and one by one compare the target value x with each element. If x matches with an element, return the index of that element. If x doesn’t match with any of the elements after checking the entire list, return -1. The time complexity of the Linear Search algorithm is O(n) . Interval Search: Interpolation Search Interpolation Search is an improvement over Binary Search for instances where the values in a sorted array are uniformly distributed. Approach: Calculate the value of pos (the probe position) using the formula. If it is a match, return the index of the item, and exit. If the item is less than the element at arr[pos] , calculate the probe position of the left sub-array. Otherwise, calculate the same in the right sub-array. Repeat until a match is found or the sub-array reduces to zero. Probe Position Formula: pos = lo + ((x - arr[lo]) * (hi - lo)) / (arr[hi] - arr[lo]) where: arr : array where elements need to be searched. x : element to be searched. lo : starting index in arr. hi : ending index in arr. Time Complexity: If elements are uniformly distributed, the complexity is O(log log n) . In the worst case, it can take up to O(n) . Hash Tables and Hash Functions Hash tables rely on hash functions to map keys to specific slots or indices in an array. Let's explore a common technique for creating a hash function. The Division Method Definition: In the division method, we map a key k into one of m slots by taking the remainder of k divided by m . The hash function is: h(k) = k mod m Example: If the hash table has size m = 12 and the key is k = 100 , then h(k) = 100 mod 12 = 4. When choosing the value for m (the size of the table), there are some important guidelines: m should not be a power of 2. m should be a prime number not too close to an exact power of 2. Summary In this lesson, we covered the fundamentals of searching and hashing. We learned about two main types of searching algorithms: Sequential Search (like Linear Search) which checks elements one by one, and Interval Search (like Interpolation Search) which is optimized for sorted, uniformly distributed data. We also introduced the concept of Hash Functions , specifically the Division Method , which uses the modulo operator to map keys to table indices.
